clinicalPearls: A severe sclerosing dysplasia marked by massive, progressive hyperostosis and sclerosis of the skull and facial bones with striking facial distortion (leontiasis ossea)
The long bones show diaphyseal widening with loss of the normal tubulation, giving a club-shaped appearance
Associated with variants affecting sclerostin (SOST) signalling, which normally restrains WNT-driven bone formation, so its loss leads to relentless bone overgrowth
Progressive narrowing of skull-base foramina causes cranial-nerve compression, with visual loss, hearing loss and facial palsy
Nasal obstruction from facial bony overgrowth and encroachment on the airway can occur early
Raised intracranial pressure may develop as the cranial vault thickens and the foramen magnum narrows
Management is largely supportive and surgical, with decompression of narrowed cranial-nerve foramina and the foramen magnum, but bone tends to reform and outcomes remain guarded
reference.pathophysiology: Craniodiaphyseal dysplasia is driven by defective sclerostin activity; sclerostin, the product of SOST, normally inhibits the WNT/beta-catenin pathway and thereby limits osteoblastic bone formation. When this brake is lost, unchecked WNT signalling produces extreme, continuous bone deposition. In the craniofacial skeleton this yields gross hyperostosis and sclerosis with grotesque facial thickening, while in the appendicular skeleton the diaphyses widen and lose their normal shape. The expanding cranial bone progressively narrows neural foramina and the foramen magnum, compressing cranial nerves and the brainstem and raising intracranial pressure, which accounts for the serious neurological complications that dominate the clinical course.
additionalInvestigations: Skull and facial CT to map hyperostosis, foraminal narrowing and foramen magnum diameter
Skeletal survey demonstrating diaphyseal widening and loss of tubulation
Cranial-nerve assessment including audiometry and formal visual testing
Neuroimaging and intracranial pressure evaluation when raised pressure is suspected
Molecular genetic testing of the sclerostin/WNT pathway to establish the diagnosis
Airway assessment where nasal or upper-airway obstruction is present
redFlags: Progressive visual loss from optic canal narrowing requiring urgent assessment
Signs of raised intracranial pressure or brainstem compression from foramen magnum stenosis
Rapidly worsening hearing loss or facial weakness indicating foraminal compression
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is poor in severe cases because of progressive cranial-nerve compression, raised intracranial pressure and the tendency of decompressed bone to reform; early and repeated surgical intervention may preserve function but does not halt the underlying overgrowth.
pitfalls: Delaying decompressive surgery until cranial-nerve deficits, especially visual loss, are irreversible
Confusing the condition with milder sclerosing dysplasias and underestimating its progressive course
Overlooking foramen magnum stenosis and the risk of brainstem compression
Failing to anticipate re-growth of bone after surgical decompression
references: Resnick's Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders
management: Largely surgical and supportive management, as no medical therapy halts the sclerostin-driven bone overgrowth
Serial cranial and skull-base surgical decompression to relieve cranial-nerve compression and raised intracranial pressure, accepting that decompressed bone tends to reform
Regular cranial-nerve surveillance with audiometry, formal visual assessment for optic compression, and monitoring for facial palsy
Monitoring and neurosurgical management of raised intracranial pressure as the vault thickens and the foramen magnum narrows
Airway management for nasal and upper-airway obstruction from facial bony overgrowth
Multidisciplinary care spanning clinical genetics, neurosurgery, ophthalmology, ENT and audiology
Genetic counselling for the family regarding the sclerostin and WNT pathway defect
